name: Threat Modeling Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building threat modeling — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary threat modeling tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building threat modeling — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary threat modeling tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Surface known limitations of a chosen threat modeling approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
2. When threat modeling decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
3. Check that threat modeling terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
4. Before starting threat modeling work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
5. State assumptions about threat modeling explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
6. Keep threat modeling changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
7. Document any non-obvious threat modeling decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
8. Prefer the simplest threat modeling approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
9. Keep threat modeling outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
10. Validate threat modeling outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
11. Re-check edge cases relevant to threat modeling (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not silently drop threat modeling edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of threat modeling correctness.
- Avoid mixing unrelated threat modeling concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not apply generic threat modeling advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for threat modeling, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
